Morality is what the world looks like from one particular angle, not a separate domain the world contains — the angle at which one parcel of Substance registers another as something that persists, is distinct from itself, and can be affected across an exchange that cannot be undone. That angle is not optional for any subject complex enough to model itself and register others. Persisting subjects meeting persisting subjects is already the subject matter of morality, before any code is written. The moral is not a layer added on top of the physical or the social. It is what reality looks like from within, to subjects who have become capable of recognizing one another.

Morality is therefore real in the way its constituents are real. Persistence, distinction, and asymmetric exchange are all real. Their conjunction — a subject meeting a subject across time and space without passing through it — is real. What moral discourse reports on, neither conventional nor projected, is what Substance, moving, actually does when it encounters other Substance. Codes and theories of morality are not inventing the subject matter; they are attempts to navigate it, and they can do so well or badly. What they cannot do is create or abolish what they describe. Morality existed as soon as there were two subjects who could meet. It will exist as long as there are.

*The anchor is not relative.* A stance-involving morality invites the immediate worry that it is therefore a relative one — true-for-me, true-for-you, with nothing underneath. It is not, and the reason is a single fact no subject can coherently stand outside. Each subject is certain of its own aversion to its own suffering — not as an empirical generalization scrutiny might overturn, but in the way §2.2.1 catches the denier of change in the act of changing. To entertain, sincerely, *perhaps I am indifferent to whether I suffer* is already to have a stake in how the entertaining goes — the aversion is exhibited in any attempt to deny it. Where the *cogito* for change catches the denier in the act of changing, this catches the subject in the act of caring. The certainty is first-person and apodictic, and it is the fixed point a stance-involving account needs: a floor that is not voted on, because no one can elect indifference to their own collapse.

That certainty has structural content, and naming it converts the negative anchor into a positive one. That content is broader than suffering — it is a subject's capacity to be averse to particular experiences and outcomes, including ones not actual but merely possible. Suffering — in the paradigm psychological case this account can claim cleanly — is one form that capacity takes when an aversive outcome is occurrent: the experienced recoil as one's field of live possibility contracts, branches thinning, the modal depth §8.9 identifies with freedom dropping toward zero. It is the experiencing and the aversion that constitute it, not the contraction as such — which is why a field narrowed while experience is suspended, as under anesthesia, is no harm to a subject not there to register it, while a subject whose body is unhurt but whose possibilities are foreclosed, and who is averse to that, has a stake regardless of any pain. The capacity's positive face is the field held maximally open. What the certain aversion is certain *of*, read forward rather than away, is maximum possibility: not the absence of pain but the optimum the avoidance points at. *Status:* the step that reads the aversion forward — into maximum possibility rather than into mere cessation — is defended by fit with the §8.9 identification of freedom with modal depth (Principle 5), not derived stance-free from the certainty itself; what the apodictic anchor certifies on its own is the subject's recoil: its aversion to the contraction of its field, not the contraction as such, and reading its positive face as the field held maximally open is licensed by that identification, not extracted from the certainty alone. This keeps the account objective without making it stance-independent — the anchor concerns subjects' own modal fields and would vanish with the last subject, yet it is not stance-determined, exactly as the language case below shows a standard can be real and binding without stance-free backup. The certainty secures only the first person; it reaches you not by acquaintance with your pain but through the one-place-to-two-place upgrade developed below — once I model you as a subject of the same structural kind, your collapse is a fact about the structure I actually inhabit, and the anchor binding me to my own continuation binds me to yours.

The question is then what grounds the encounter in the first place — what it means for there to be subjects capable of meeting subjects at all.

*The conatus structure of life.* Before there are subjects meeting subjects, there is life persisting. A living system is the active avoidance of dissolution, not a current that merely happens to avoid it. A system that did not pursue its own continuation would not persist long enough to count as alive. The avoidance is what being an organism structurally consists in — it isn't added on as a preference. Spinoza (1677, *Ethics* III) named this the *conatus* — the striving by which each finite mode perseveres in its being. Hans Jonas (1966, 1984) and Evan Thompson (2007), working from biology rather than metaphysics, reached the same result: self-maintaining systems generate their own norms because self-maintenance establishes a perspective from which outcomes are better or worse *for the system itself*.

Critics have pressed whether this move dissolves the is/ought question too quickly. Bedau (1992) argues that biological self-maintenance licenses at most a weak functional normativity — what is good-for-the-organism in the teleological sense, not yet what is good full stop. Philosophers of biology (Godfrey-Smith 1996; Di Paolo 2005) have raised parallel worries about the Jonas/Thompson line in particular — whether *self-maintaining* carries the normative weight the argument places on it. The response consolidates these: the conatus structure is not yet morality. It is the material from which morality becomes possible, as *Vulnerability registers* below makes explicit. What the *is* of life delivers is constitutive normativity at the organism's own level of persistence; what morality adds is the registration of that structure *in another subject*.

The bridge from functional to moral normativity has a specific structural shape, and naming it directly is what the Bedau/Godfrey-Smith/Di Paolo line presses for. Functional normativity is *one-place*: it concerns what is good for system S relative to S's own persistence-conditions. The norm is internal to S and does not yet bind anyone but S. Moral normativity is *two-place*: it concerns what subject A owes subject B, how A's actions register with B's persistence-conditions and B's with A's. The move from one-place to two-place amounts to a structural upgrade in what is being normed, not the addition of social complexity to a fixed normative kind. What performs the upgrade is mutual registration. When A has reached the recursive depth at which it can model B as a closure-plus-throughput recursion with persistence-conditions of the same structural kind as A's own, A's deliberation about its own actions is no longer adequately described by reference to A's persistence-conditions alone. B's persistence-conditions are now items in A's structural environment that A's model has registered. An A that ignores them is not merely indifferent to B; A is refusing what its own registration already contains. Having modeled B as a subject of the same structural kind — persistence-conditions as real as A's own — the recoil that floors A's stake in its own continuation reaches B by a constraint of consistency, not by a new sentiment. What grounds the stake is the feature *being a subject with the capacity to be averse to particular experiences and outcomes*; the first person is how A accesses that feature — A is certain of its own aversions — not what gives it weight. Strip the indexical — *that it is A's* — and the stake either survives, because the feature was doing the work and the same feature is present in B, or it evaporates as bare preference. An A that weighs its own collapse while refusing B's the same weight is then not merely indifferent to B; it is prizing the ground only where it is indexed to itself, mistaking its access to the ground for the ground. The neglect is an inconsistency in what A has already claimed on its own behalf, not a miscalculation of payoff. *Status:* the load-bearing premise of this step — that indexicality is access, not ground: a reason either grounds in a generalizable feature or evaporates as bare preference — is named here at its point of use, because everything universal in the two-place norm rides on it; a committed agent-relativist of the internal-reasons kind denies exactly this, and the account defends it by fit (Principle 5) together with the apodictic anchor above, not as stance-free proof. The two-place norm is what one-place normativity becomes when the subjects holding it have started modeling each other accurately; it is not a separate kind of thing layered on top of functional norms but the same constitutive normativity tracking a more inclusive structure. *Ought* in the moral sense names what falls out of accurate modeling at this depth, not what is read off biological function. No Humean derivation crosses any gap because none is attempted: the crossing is a constraint of consistency, and it binds any subject that makes a claim on its own behalf. The one subject it does not reach is the one who makes no claim on its own behalf at all — the purely indexical, structurally insulated egoist who will bite the bullet on its own collapse too. That figure is the limit case §8.12.5 names, held off others not by conviction but by withdrawn consent and the structure cooperation builds; the floor binds every participant and is escaped only by refusing to participate. Bedau is right that biological self-maintenance alone delivers only weak functional normativity. Godfrey-Smith and Di Paolo are right to press whether *self-maintaining* could carry the load on its own. The structural account agrees on both points and locates the upgrade precisely where intersubjective registration brings the further structure into view: the additional content moral normativity has, beyond functional normativity, is the content of a model that has accurately taken in another subject of the same kind.

This is what dissolves the is/ought question at its source. *Life wants to avoid dissolution* looks like a descriptive claim that would need to be bridged to a normative one. It is not. The wanting and the being-alive are the same structural fact described from two angles: from outside, the system avoids dissolution; from inside its own structure, it must avoid dissolution to remain itself. There is no gap between the *is* and the *must* — the *must* is what the *is* of life consists in. No derivation crosses the is/ought divide because life's *is* already carries the constitutive normativity intersubjective registration picks up.

Thermodynamic selection underwrites the universality. The default of any medium with T, S, and Φ is dissolution — gradients flatten, organization decays, exchange disperses. Prigogine and Nicolis (1977) showed how far-from-equilibrium organization can produce self-maintaining systems that dissipate gradients; Schrödinger (1944) had already named the point by calling life a process that feeds on negative entropy. Any persistent self-maintaining system is therefore, by what *self-maintaining* structurally means, actively resisting that default. The claim is not biological and does not depend on Darwinian mechanisms specifically; natural selection as we know it is one sorting mechanism among possible others, an Earth-specific instantiation of a deeper principle: only avoidance-pursuing currents persist, because persistence *is* avoidance of dissolution. The §7.6 cycle argument secures the reach: T, S, and Φ are not contingent features of this epoch but conditions that recur wherever the universe iterates, so conatus-structured life is a feature of any current the recurrence produces. The shared aversions cooperation generalizes are not parochial to terrestrial biology; they are features any life in any universe could not lack.

From shared aversion, cooperation follows necessarily. Life that cooperates exposes itself to fewer of the outcomes it must avoid. Cooperation requires reliable coordination. Reliable coordination requires norms — reciprocate, do not defect, do not harm cooperators. Those norms stabilize into morality. No premise outside the structural conditions of life-in-relation enters at any step. Morality is what happens when life, pursuing its constitutive avoidance, encounters other life pursuing the same.

The question is then how one parcel of life comes to register another — how Substance, meeting Substance, comes to register itself as such.

*Self-modeling and the registration of vulnerability.* For the encounter to come into view within a subject, the subject must be able to model itself. A subject that registers its own exposure to harm — its own persistence as the kind of thing that can be broken, its own position as the kind of thing that can be reached — is also the kind of subject that can register another subject as standing in the same kind of relation to harm. Empathy, before it is a feeling, is this second registration: another subject's exposure, internally tracked (Hoffman 2000; Batson 2011; Decety and Jackson 2004; Singer and Lamm 2009; de Waal 2008). It is not yet morality. It is the material from which morality becomes possible — the moment at which one parcel of Substance begins to model another as persisting, distinct, and reachable. Vulnerability in this sense is positional, not metaphorical: to be reachable is to occupy a position within Space, at a moment in Time, as Substance that persists through the exchange. It is not a cultural ornament added to an otherwise indifferent structure.

That registration gives morality its vocabulary. To *draw a boundary* is a spatial act (this side, not that side), made at a moment (from now on), by someone who persists as the one who drew it — Space, Time, Substance, already named in the verb. To *hold* a boundary requires persistence against the pull to violate it; to *cross* a boundary is to violate a limit that was supposed to hold. Morality, before it is codified in any system, is the practice of drawing, holding, and honoring the limits that register the reality of another subject.

A consequence follows for a question that has organized meta-ethics for three centuries.

*The is/ought question reframed.* What does not follow from any of this is a valid inference from *is* to *ought*. Hume correctly identified the inference; a century of meta-ethics then misread his observation as a metaphysical gap in need of a bridge. It is not a gap but a category boundary, and the demand for a derivation was always the wrong thing to want. Descriptive claims report what is the case. Prescriptive claims do something else — they guide, commit, coordinate. Oughts are not conclusions of derivations. Arguments articulate features of the situation; those features compel; the compulsion is what the ought consists in. An argument can be pressed indefinitely and still convert no one: articulation can turn a subject's attention toward a feature of the situation, but it cannot perform the conversion from *is* to *ought* on the subject's behalf. That conversion happens only within the one to be moved, when the feature engages a field already weighted to register it — what an argument hands across is the feature, never the compulsion. The compulsion is the affective pointer the body's already-valenced modal field (§8.3, §8.2) produces when it reads its own possibility space — the felt-best branch within the field, weighted by the body's own stake in each branch.

That reframes the is/ought question as an alignment problem. An ought lands on someone only when it is articulated at the level of moral development their uptake can register. A four-year-old and a philosopher do not receive the same argument the same way; a subject whose empathic equipment has been blunted by trauma, ideology, or structural neglect may not receive it at all. Failures of moral uptake — psychopathy, dissociation, radicalization, trauma, severe self-interest — sit in the gap between articulated reasons and the compulsion they should produce, not in any failure of derivation. Moral progress happens less through new inferences than through the articulation of features previously unattended: abolition, expansions of the moral circle, recognition of harms to those who cannot complain.

*The compulsion has more than one grip.* Because an ought is a compulsion rather than a conclusion, what matters is not that one argument reach everyone but that the situation’s features find some purchase on the subject at all — and there is more than one surface they can catch on. One subject is moved because an authority it trusts has spoken, the feature arriving with the standing of someone entitled to command; another by consequence, the aversion to penalty or loss the valenced field (§8.3, §8.2) registers the moment a branch is run forward far enough to show it; another by standing among others whose regard it needs, reputation being the social face of the same persistence-stake; another by a principle it has made its own, so that to violate it would break with what the subject has identified with — the self-legislated grip Frankfurt’s volitional necessity (§8.12.1) names. They are not rungs on a ladder in the sense of a maturity contest, obedience beneath and principle above — no grip is disqualified for being the one that happens to reach a given subject; they are different places the one compulsion takes hold. Yet they do fall into an intuitive order, not by dignity but by reach — by how much of the field the subject has come to register. A being that models only itself is answerable mostly to what befalls it; as its registration widens — to intimates, to a community, to a society, to subjects it will never meet — the grip that moves it shifts with it, toward principles that hold for everyone it has learned to count. The order is a shadow the widening circle of registration casts across the grips, not a ranking of the grips themselves. Most subjects, in any case, are reachable through several grips at once, in proportions that shift with what is at stake and with how far their registration currently reaches.

*The grips are not equal in what they can correct.* Consequence, reputation, and principle each carry an internal check: a subject moved by them can ask whether the penalty is real, whether the regard is deserved, whether the principle survives being made general — and can revise the verdict against the answer. The authority grip carries no such check. Its content is exhausted by *someone entitled to command has spoken*, so the only question it can raise from the inside is what was in fact commanded, and that is settled by interpretation rather than by anything the situation itself supplies. A morality anchored solely in authority therefore has no court of appeal within itself: when its directives are unclear, conflict with one another, or run against what its adherents have otherwise come to register, it can move only by disputing the text, never by testing the directive against the subjects it governs. This is a structural property of the grip, not a verdict on the truth of any particular authority, and it predicts what the record plainly shows — that moral traditions anchored in a fixed ancient command remain perennially contested over what their own morality requires, carry directives their later adherents come to judge indefensible and must reinterpret or explain away, and cannot close those disputes from within, the only internal resource being a return to the same underdetermined source. “Because God said so” is the limit case: it places the whole of moral weight in the fact of the command, and inherits the limitation entire. What a recognition- or principle-grounded morality can do that an authority-grounded one cannot is check a directive against the registered reality of the affected subject — the apodictic aversion of §2.2.1, a standard no text can revoke — which is why moral progress has tended to run by re-grounding inherited commands in the subjects they concern rather than in the authority that issued them. What they share is the phenomenology: each delivers the same felt *I ought to*, because each is the valenced field reading its own possibility space through a different one of its channels. This is why the alignment problem is really many problems — to move a subject one must articulate the feature at whatever surface its uptake registers — and why moral formation is less the supplying of a correct argument than the finding, in a given subject, of which grip the compulsion still has.

Morality must therefore be cultivated. Family, punishment, attachment, reciprocity, education, imitation, narrative, and institutional design hone the rough equipment biology supplies. Which grip takes hold most readily varies from subject to subject — one most responsive to empathy, another to reputation, another to consistency, another chiefly to consequences — and formation works by strengthening whichever a given subject already has. The hard cases fit this picture better than a stronger realism does: they do not show that the exposure of subjects is unreal; they show that uptake can be blunted, fragmented, or severed. Because freedom is modal depth (§8.9), that blunting is at the same time a structural narrowing of the agent's own field of live options — a graded reduction of agency, not an all-or-nothing exemption from it — which is why such failures modulate the response a breakdown calls for without dissolving responsibility: the agent's contribution to causal history is degraded, not erased, and the harm done to the subjects on the other side of it remains fully real (the Modally Compatibilist Responsibility corollary, §9.12). This cultivation is not application bolted on downstream of the theory — as though the account of what an ought is could be finished first and the forming of uptake left to educators afterward. Because an ought exists only as a compulsion that has come to fire in a subject, the conditions under which it comes to fire are part of what the ought is, not a practical addendum to it. An account that delivers the structure of the moral relation but stays silent on how the compulsion is cultivated has given the skeleton of the ought and omitted its mode of existence; a meta-ethics complete on paper can still leave the ought it describes inert.

The shape of moral norms is visible in a nearby case: language (§8.10). No one designed English. It emerged from speakers-in-relation, constrained by what coordination among speakers necessarily requires — phonemes distinguishable from one another, utterances ordered in time, meanings persisting across the utterance long enough to be received. No Platonic entity decrees that English plurals take *-s*, and yet within a linguistic community there are genuinely right and wrong ways to speak. Errors miscommunicate. Ungrammatical constructions fail. Misleading usages damage coordination. A speaker who declares that *water* henceforth means *fire* has not redefined the word; they have stepped outside the coordination that makes speech work. The structure did not bend to accommodate them.

Two features of this case matter. Language is *stance-involving*: grammatical facts are facts about speakers and hearers, not about a speaker-less reality. Remove all speakers and there are no grammatical facts left — not grammatical facts stripped of observers, but no facts at all, because grammar's content is exhaustively about coordination among stance-bearers. And language is *not stance-determined*: no individual speaker, and no collective consensus, can unilaterally redefine what English is. The structure is real, binding, teachable, enforceable, answerable to facts about how communication works among creatures like us — and none of that reality depends on the existence of stance-independent linguistic properties. There are no such properties. There does not need to be.

Morality works the same way. Moral facts are stance-involving because their content is exhaustively about agents-in-relation — what one subject does to another, what persists across exchange, what one owes another who is vulnerable in the ways one is oneself vulnerable. There is no moral fact left once the stances are removed, any more than there is a grammatical fact left once the speakers are removed. But moral facts are not stance-determined either: no individual agent, and no collective consensus, can unilaterally declare that betrayal is fine or that gratuitous cruelty is acceptable. The structure of coordination among mutually exposed subjects generates determinate content that individual stances can violate but cannot dismiss.

This is the answer to the robust realist who holds that real moral facts must be *stance-independent* in the strong sense — independent of all stances, collective as well as individual. Language shows that stance-independence is not what distinguishes real standards from fake ones: the standards of a living language are genuinely binding, objective within their domain, answerable to facts — and entirely constituted by the coordination of stance-bearers. The same possibility is available for morality. Stance-involving does not mean unreal; it means real in the way standards about coordination among stance-bearers are real: objectively, bindingly, without needing stance-free Platonic backup. The normative pull the realist takes as evidence for stance-independent facts is the pull the intersubjective structure produces, and can be accounted for without the further posit.

Two specific patterns follow as predictions falsifiable against the empirical record. The negative formulation of reciprocity — *do not do to others what they would not have you do* — should recur across cultures that share nothing else, because it carves the structural floor of non-corrosion that any encounter between persisting subjects requires; the positive formulation, which depends on attunement to throughput conditions that vary across forms of life, should appear later and be more variable. Harm-symmetric reciprocity — refusal of mistreatment, punishment of defectors, consolation of distress — should be biologically broader than flourishing-symmetric prosociality, because the affect-family registers damage more legibly across currents than it registers deepening: pain, fear, and grief broadcast in forms more reliably shared than the forms in which joy opens.

If this is how morality comes into view and how it spreads, then wherever its conditions obtain, its characteristic pattern should obtain with them.
